retainedText: mash. But it reached, and continues to reach, the people who needed it. In her liner notes for “Horses,” Smith wrote about “new risks etched forever in a cold system of wax,” and the album has been an example for generations of songwriters — some to emulate its sound, but many more to take up its insistence on self-discovery, its “sea of possibilities.” Below, Patti Smith, her band and their musical heirs offer some insights on half a century of listening to “Horses.” Side 1 Side 1 Gloria [] [] Patti Smith We had “Land.” Then one day we were in the practice room, making a set list, and I said, “I’d love it if we had another song that had simple chords.” I wanted something I could riff off of. And Lenny said, “Well, there’s ‘Gloria.’” And I was like, “Is that a good one?” And he said, “It’s the best.” It freed me up in a certain way to do a song like “Gloria,” and not be hung up with the fact that it was written from a male point of view. [] Lenny Kaye (guitarist and songwriter, Patti Smith Group) Patti would do a poem, and then we’d segue into a song. And then we would use the song as a jumping-off point for Patti’s magical journeys — wherever she would take us and the audience — and follow along and see where you wound up. And hopefully, at the end of the narration, get back to the song. [] Clive Davis (record executive) When I first heard “Gloria,” it blew me away. In well over 90 percent of artist auditions, I always looked for hit songs. Here, her uniqueness and originality knocked me out. Of course I wanted hits, but I always appreciated edge and uniqueness. Sly Stone wrote hits, but he was unique and had edge. Joplin was to have hits but she defined someone with edge. Could Patti Smith have a hit? I didn’t care! [] Thurston Moore (musician, Sonic Youth) There’s something very postmodern about it. They transcend the cover song into a wholly other composition that is their own. [A black-and-white photo of five members of a band playing on a very small stage.] From left: Ivan Kral, Smith, Jay Dee Daugherty on drums, John Cale and Kaye. Richard E. Aaron/Redferns, via Getty Images [] John Cale (musician; producer, “Horses”) We started recording and I noticed that there were some problems with the instruments. We spent a lot of time early on in the sessions getting intonation and everything else right, until finally we just said, “The hell with it — let’s call S.I.R. [Studio Instrument Rentals] and rent.” And I felt really like a brute, because they were obviously so attached to the instruments. In the end everybody adjusted and it helped a lot. Most of the time, I was really trying to stay away. It was very important to let Patti do the creating and watch what happens then. [] Patti Smith I didn’t understand the recording beast. I didn’t understand how records were put together. I didn’t understand the possibilities of technology. I just wanted people to hear us as we were, not some overly enhanced or sanitized version of who we were. [] Bruce Springsteen (musician) The album starts with [] probably the greatest opening line of anyone’s debut album in rock ’n’ roll. [] Courtney Love (musician) Best [expletive] opening line ever! [] Bono (musician) “Jesus died for somebody’s sins, but not mine.” Hard for this 17-year-old to get past that. Is this a confession? Is this a statement of fact or fear? An invocation or invitation for all of us who felt fallen? Is this defiance against the priesthood? I suppose it’s all of the above. Back then I couldn’t believe that she could take an early rock ’n’ soul classic like Van Morrison’s “Gloria” (national anthem in Ireland!) and dare to reimagine, reboot and refloat it as salacious stalking fire breathing punk prayer, smudging the lines between the sexual and the spiritual. In a certain sense this album offered me as a singer and the band a manifesto for how I will go about the next 49 years. [] Skin (musician, Skunk Anansie) When my mum left the room, I would change the radio to Radio 1, the BBC. She came back when “Gloria” came on with that very first lyric, walked over and just switched it off. I didn’t know who it was, whose record it was. But in my head, that very first lyric kept wandering around. That was a lyric that sparked in me that I didn’t have to do what my parents told me to do, and also that other people thought religion wasn’t good. That very first song was a spark for so many things in my life. [] Florence Welch (musician, Florence + the Machine) “Gloria” is free-flowing, but [] the hook is so solid. It’s like taking something masculine and swaggering — you feel all that aggression — but by the end, it’s just ecstatic. An ecstatic religious experience, almost. [A black-and-white photo of Patti Smith standing before a microphone and gazing skyward, her hands help up before her.] Richard E. Aaron/Redferns, via Getty Images [] Lenny Kaye Gloria is really about acceleration. You know, [] every time another section comes in, you can feel the band pop the clutch. [] Jimmy Iovine (record executive and producer) The improvisation, many times, goes right to the cliff, and then it just manages to scale that cliff and handle it. On “Gloria,” you feel like, oh, this can go wrong. Even while listening to the record for the 10th time, you feel that this could go wrong. To be able to land that is pretty remarkable. [] Courtney Love She saved my life. I was in juvenile hall about to go to foster care. And in one month, two of my counselors — cool hippies from Eugene [Ore.] — gave me “Horses.” And then my foster father gave me “Horses” the same month. Three guys gave it to me, and they said, “This reminds me of you, Courtney.” It just changed things. I was like, there are other people like me in the world. I’d never heard anything like it. And I’d never seen a woman like that. “What the [expletive] is she doing? I don’t know, but I want to do that too.” Listen on Spotify, Apple Music or YouTube Side 1 Redondo Beach [] [] Patti Smith I wrote it at the Chelsea Hotel. I had a rare argument with my sister and she disappeared, I think she went to Coney Island. But I got this frightened feeling that something had happened to her. I wrote it as a poem and I used to read it in poetry readings. And then with Richard [Sohl] and Lenny, it evolved as a little reggae song. [A black-and-white photo of a woman leaning out on a small balcony above a New York City street.] Smith at the Chelsea Hotel on 23rd Street. David Gahr/Getty Images [] Lenny Kaye We were fascinated by reggae. I would often in the ’70s go out to Brooklyn, to the West Indian neighborhoods, and go into record stores and ask them to play me every single. [] Jay Dee Daugherty (drummer, Patti Smith Group) I hadn’t listened to enough reggae and ska and stuff like that to really feel like I knew what I was doing. I just remember not being able to figure it out. I think it sounds very [] very halting. [] Michael Stipe (musician, R.E.M.) She was brought up by radio in the ’50s — the Shirelles and the Ronettes. If you listen to the music and the voice and the rhythm of the voice, there’s a lot of similarity there to girl groups, that kind of [] energy and cadence. [] Bruce Springsteen She’ll very often juxtapose very dark lyrics against a brighter melody or a brighter arrangement. I like the way that that was conceived and balanced. [] Ana Da Silva (musician, the Raincoats) It was a voice of a woman in a way that I had never heard before. And then there’s that introductory line: “Redondo Beach is a beach where women love other women.” That at that time was just extraordinary. It wasn’t the statement itself. It was just the way she put it. And made that whole issue of a woman loving another woman a beautiful thing, which wasn’t always seen as a beautiful thing — still isn’t, but in those days, even worse. And then I went to see her play, at the Roundhouse in London. She came onstage in a such a strong way with boots, and she put a flower in her mouth and spat it out, and all the petals went everywhere. It was like saying goodbye to wishy-washy attitudes, and let’s fight for things that are important. [] Billy Idol (musician) I didn’t realize that “Redondo Beach” would be about female love, necessarily. A lot of people who were struggling with gender identity were very much part of punk rock. In our world, that’s what we were looking for — a sense of freedom that you could own your own sexuality. And there she is singing about that, ahead of everybody else. In the liner notes to “Horses,” she says she’s “beyond gender,” and that’s what I see now. Listen on Spotify, Apple Music or YouTube Side 1 Birdland [] [] Patti Smith I was completely green. I had never worked with a producer. If John couldn’t win, he would step back and challenge me. “OK, you want to improvise ‘Birdland’? You want to wing it? Then really do it.” I was not easy to challenge because I was very self-assured. I had more self-assurance than talent, perhaps. When I achieved something, I could see it in his face. It gave me a sense of accomplishment, because if you can please another artist, that’s a high goal — if you cannot placate, but inspire. [A black-and-white photo of two musicians, back to back and grinning.] From left: Richard Sohl and Smith. Suzan Carson/Michael Ochs Archive, via Getty Images [] Lenny Kaye The song started as a little three-minute poem to musical accompaniment by Richard Sohl and my wah-wah pedal. And as it progressed, we kept pushing it further. And a lot of that was John. [] John Cale I had an appreciation of the language that she spoke and the emotions that were there. And I really didn’t want to disturb them. I wanted to let the thing be real and natural. [] Skin [] The layers of guitars on that one — that feels like what she’s feeling in her head. Like it’s all this stuff, all this information, all this wildness, all this crazy stuff coming out as a howl. [] Bruce Springsteen At the end of “Birdland,” she goes into [] a little doo-wop riff. Patti was born in ’46, so she had that in her DNA. She was both a revolutionary and a classicist. [] Michael Stipe “Birdland” was the pivotal moment for me as a 15-year-old. That’s when I sat up straight and went, what the [expletive] is this? It’s like I was hearing a new language in my own language. When you read her poetry, you realize these are sometimes drawn from real stories. But her take on it is completely mind-bending. It becomes this whole other thing about grief and love and transcendence and the possibility of life beyond life — the importance and the fragility of life, but then what comes next? I mean, that’s a whole lot to jam into even a nine-minute song. [A black-and-white photo of Patti Smith from 1975 in a coat and scarf reaching upward with one hand and holding papers in the other. She’s standing before a microphone, in front of a brick wall with a framed painting on it.] Richard E. Aaron/Redferns, via Getty Images [] Florence Welch She contains this wide-eyed, innocent, almost girlishness in some of her phrases, especially at the beginning of “Birdland.” There’s a way she describes [] the stars as being filmed with butter, it’s so innocent and beautiful. And then there is this [] swaggering masculinity that’s so present too. And she switches between the two in a way that has been really inspirational to me. [] Adele Bertei (writer, director and musician, the Contortions) “As if someone had spread butter on all the fine points of the stars, because when he looked up, they started to slip.” I mean, what?! Women never talked like that in rock ’n’ roll. It was like Yeats meets Jim Morrison meets this woman embodied in this female spirit. She ripped away the straitjackets from our imaginations and let us know that we didn’t have to be these female gendered archetypes. Listen on Spotify, Apple Music or YouTube Side 1 Free Money [] [] Patti Smith So many people think it’s a love song. I wrote it as [] “Oh baby,” as if perhaps it is, but it was really for my mother. My family struggled financially, sometimes to the point of not having enough food on the table. They worked hard their whole life. They couldn’t really support me. But I never lacked love. [A black-and-white photo of Patti Smith with messy brown hair, captured in close-up staring intently at the camera, in front of a gauzy window curtain. ] Bill Rowntree/Mirrorpix, via Getty Images [] Thurston Moore “Free Money” opens so beautifully about having this dream of finding a lottery ticket under your pillow, and the idea of this gift which will liberate you, but there’s actually something very illusory about it at the same time. It’s almost this kind of Buddhist purview in a way. I mean, there’s no such thing as free money. It’s an oxymoron. [] Skin There are those lines: [] “Every night before I rest my head / See those dollar bills go swirling ’round my bed.” I’m from a very poor background. I definitely remember that one hitting me like, “Yeah girl, I’m there with you.” [] Lenny Kaye A lot of the songs — “Free Money” for instance — didn’t start as songs. They started as Patti singing over a chord progression with an idea that she had. We would call them “fields” — fields of exploration where we’d recycle the chords. The song would emerge from the repeated playings. “Free Money” is just [] A minor, F, G, F, G. On and on and on. And pretty soon, it got parts. It told us where it wanted to go. [] Sammy Hagar (musician; covered “Free Money” on his self-titled 1977 album) My producer at that time, John Carter — he signed Tina Turner to Capitol — played me “Free Money.” And I really didn’t know about Patti at that time. I’m going, “This is a passionate love song.” I wasn’t a punk guy. So I thought, well, let’s make it into just a really passionate love song and kind of take the punk out of it. I grew up poor as [expletive], so I related to those lyrics. My mom raised four children with no education, picking fruit. My mother never owned a home until I bought it for her. It was on my list of the first things I was going to do with any money I got — and I did. So tell Patti that dream came true. [A black-and-white photo of a woman and two men seated at a restaurant table, with drinks before them, deep in conversation.] From left: Kaye, Smith and Sohl. [] Johnny Marr (musician, the Smiths) I was sneaking into gigs at Manchester University. “Free Money” was the track that the mixing guys were playing in between sets because it was so catchy. The sound was just very — there’s no other word for it really than hip. The band weren’t hiding behind production. The producer wasn’t hiding behind tricks. The singer wasn’t hiding behind harmonies. [] Thurston Moore In some ways the beautiful epicenter of “Horses” is [] Richard Sohl’s piano playing. In the early recordings that are available, when it’s just Patti and Lenny, it’s pretty scratchy and raw. But when Richard Sohl comes into the band, he brings a musical cohesion. Listen on Spotify, Apple Music or YouTube A Life-Changing Artist “She taught me how to dress, in a way that was like, get [expletive] from the dumpster and make your own look. She never didn’t look cool.” — [] Courtney Love musician “I’m so grateful that she was such an iconoclast. She was unlike anybody else that had come along before, and that gave people a chance to explore who they were.” —[Justin Vivian Bond] Justin Vivian Bond musician [A double exposure photo of Patti Smith with her eyes closed.] “She was a rebel, a beautiful, emotional rebel. It was like a call to do the thing that I wanted to do.” — [] Susanna Hoffs musician, the Bangles “I always say, ‘Yeah, I’m kind of a showman. But Patti’s a shaman.’” — [] Bruce Springsteen musician Side 2 Side 2 Kimberly [] [] Lenny Kaye Patti’s remembering the birth of her sister Kimberly. I believe it started like a Booker T. & the M.G.’s kind of song. [] Richard’s organ certainly leads the way. [] Billy Idol There wasn’t a lyric sheet with the original “Horses.” And “Kimberly,” I had no idea that it was about a sister of hers. I thought that she was singing to, you know, sisters as in feminism or whatever. The interplay of the musicians was fantastic. You can hear it in “Horses,” you can hear it in Television. In England we were watching what was going on in the States, and we wanted a scene of our own like that. The structure of the song is very classic. All the different parts, the way it builds up, it’s almost got a ’60s thing to it. They’re taking guitar music and refreshing it, but at the same time not falling back on prog-rock. It flows really great, but it has all those different hooks. As the song progresses, each little verse changes it. [] Johnny Marr The first song that the Smiths ever wrote, “The Hand That Rocks the Cradle,” was inspired by “Kimberly.” I knew Patti Smith was our common ground. [] Corin Tucker (musician, Sleater-Kinney) It’s deep, and it’s this interesting relationship, and it was so different than how women were historically relating to each other in pop culture. Riot grrrl was a lot about women relating to each other in different ways, in ways that were validating and re-evaluating our relationships with each other, and writing songs about each other. Having a song like that in our back pocket was super important. [] Florence Welch She’s painting the picture right in front of you. And you’re seeing all the images as she sees them. There’s a certain sermonizing quality to it as well. You really feel the deep reverence that comes through her work. [A black-and-white photo of Patti Smith (from 1976) standing before a microphone and staring. ] Jorgen Angel/Redferns, via Getty Images [] Blondshell (musician) That’s not just a love song between two sisters or from one sister to another sister, but it’s also like you can hear the weight of her saying, I’m caring for another living being right now. When I heard her say, “I feel like just some misplaced Joan of Arc,” and then later, “Your soul was like a network of spittle,” I was just like, wait a second. We’re allowed to say things like that? Songs didn’t have to just be romantic. Songs could be about family and being freaked out by an electrical storm, or holding her little sister. The diction and the cadence of how she says these things, like [] “violet violent sky.” It literally feels like a crack in the sky. [] Susanna Hoffs (musician, the Bangles) I just loved how personal it was that she’s singing about her baby sister, who she loved and adored so much, and loves and adores now. There was a tenderness and a beauty in that song that was so moving. And I just love the melody of it. There’s a little bit of 1950s influence that creeps into some of Patti’s songs. Listen on Spotify, Apple Music or YouTube Side 2 Break It Up [] [] Patti Smith The song is a homage to poetry, to Jim [Morrison], to dreaming, but it also is a little document of my friendship with Tom [Verlaine] and our process together. Tom was amazing because he wrote hundreds, if not thousands of songs, while I struggled with every one. He said, “Oh, it’s easy. Give me your notebook.” [A black-and-white photo taken at a party in 1974 captures Tom Verlaine, in a light-colored T-shirt, embracing Patti Smith, in a darker T-shirt, with a chandelier visible above them.] Tom Verlaine and Smith. Pierre Schermann/WWD and Penske Media, via Getty Images We opened up to a page where I had written about a dream that I had just had, that I was in a graveyard and there was a sculpture of a young, beautiful Prometheus lying on the ground, shackled. He had a face like Jim Morrison, and I could feel his life force inside of this statue, trapped in that marble casing. And I kept crying out, “Break it up!” It cracked and he emerged with wings and he flew away. There were other things in the notebook, some conversation bits and things. [] “Don’t talk to me that way. I’m not listening.” Only Tom would put that in a song. I wrote it, but I would have never put it in a song. He said to me, “Don’t be afraid to steal from yourself.” [] Courtney Love I love “Break It Up.” Oh my God, it’s a rock anthem! It’s a stadium anthem. [] Matt Berninger (musician, the National) It’s about mutation, and all about breaking free from yourself and your own identity, and then climbing into each other’s skin. There’s something about it that’s really sexy and visceral, and it has a chorus. You can tell it’s just really organic — people in a room finding it as they go. You can even [] hear her hitting herself in the chest sometimes. You’re literally in this woman’s brain, and then you hear all the musicians, they’re listening to her. And then it all starts to float in and becomes this collective mind — in real time, making creative split-second choices. [A black-and-white photo of Patti Smith with shaggy brown hair, from 1975, holding a cigarette between her fingers and wearing a T-shirt featuring a man with shaggy brown hair.] Vagabond Video/Getty Images [] Johnny Marr I started playing along with “Horses” as soon as I got it, and “Break It Up” was one of my favorite songs for years. [] Tom Verlaine’s playing was a million miles away from what everybody else was doing at the time. It felt like a new day for guitar playing. [] Michael Stipe Tom Verlaine and Peter [Buck from R.E.M.] were the only guitarists I could ever watch play and be completely captivated by. They become the instrument. [] Adele Bertei The musical structure of “Break It Up” mirrors a resurrection. It starts out with this quiet entombment, and then the tremor starts out the fight, and then the explosion, the ascent of when she does break through, and the whole band breaks through with her. Tom’s guitar on that song is so delicate. I explain it as a halo of birds around her incantations; it just builds and it builds. And towards the end of the song, it’s like that [] flock of birds just explodes from her heart as she transcends. Listen on Spotify, Apple Music or YouTube Side 2 Land [] [] Patti Smith The word “land” was from “Land of 1000 Dances” [the 1962 Chris Kenner song]. I loved “A Thousand and One Nights” and the idea of Scheherazade telling story after story. For a long time, “Land” went through various configurations. In one, it was almost like the history of rock ’n’ roll. Jimi Hendrix. James Brown. It would be a litany. Then I was reading “The Wild Boys” and was very influenced by William Burroughs, and Johnny [a character in the novel] hit the scene. [] Lenny Kaye There were six weeks at CBGB early in 1975 that we played Thursday through Sunday with Television, alternating sets. Johnny would be on a different adventure in “Land” every night, depending on the mood and, you know, the phases of the moon. The chords are pretty simple but as you keep playing them, you go on a journey. Sometimes we’d be playing it for a while and I’d have my eyes closed, following the path that Patti is outlining for us. At the end of the song, I’d open them and I’d think, “Where was I?” [] Bruce Springsteen On “Land,” there’s context and there’s shape and there’s form. But in spite of that, she’s into lyrical free jazz. She’s gone into some very transcendent spirit place. She was totally letting herself be seen, letting you see her. She was funny. She was not ironic. It’s all heart out on her sleeve. [A black-and-white photo of a woman holding a clutch of flowers to her chest in a bathroom.] Charlie Steiner/Getty Images [] Corin Tucker The album is so experimental. There are two nine-minute songs on it, right? Like they’re just going there. It’s built on relationships and on human interaction and on that kind of actual work. And that takes guts, and it takes crafting, and people supporting that kind of work. [] Matt Berninger Poetry is like ice skating, whereas songwriting to me feels like swimming. With songwriting, you’re down in the water and you’re really reacting to the music, whereas with poetry, you’re on the top. All through “Horses” you hear someone who is probably more comfortable in poetry starting to become a singer and a songwriter, starting to break that boundary. It’s like you literally hear her break through the ice and start swimming. [] Jimmy Iovine What I marvel about with “Horses” is her becoming a singer and recording artist from being a poet, and how she just so incredibly did that, especially in songs like “Gloria” and “Land.” They were true rock ’n’ roll songs, but she [] interpolated those songs very much like the way hip-hop is interpolated today, with all the samples. [] Patti Smith At the end of the record, when technology became my friend, I did the other voices. They were all in different personas. Some of them being desperate, some of them more in a preacher sort of way, and some just babbling, [] intentional babble. I had no idea how “Land” was going to end. We were, of course, in Jimi Hendrix’s studio. I was very moved to be in his studio, even feeling a certain amount of a mix of privilege and guilt. Because I had briefly met him on the stairs, and he was dead maybe two weeks later. It always haunted me. As we were finishing, it was like I saw him. [] “In the sheets, there was a man / Dancing around to a simple rock 'n' roll song.” That is Jimi Hendrix. That’s the end of his life. I saw him. I was almost in tears, and that’s how “Land” ended. [A black-and-white photo of a woman in a T-shirt leaning down onstage, her eyes closed.] Tom Hill/Getty Images [] Jay Dee Daugherty With “Land,” I don’t know whether it was a strategy of [our producer] John’s or not, but he kept interrupting us before we could finish it, which was quite disturbing, especially to Patti. I kind of blew up: “Let us finish a [expletive] take!” I don’t know whether it was deliberate or not, but it really brought us together as a band. “We’ll show that guy,” you know. [] Lenny Kaye The collaboration between John and our band was very fruitful. It forced us to make decisions about who we wanted to be. And that to me is what a debut album is. And the fact is that 50 years later, for whatever the strengths and flaws of the record, it’s still speaking to people. Listen on Spotify, Apple Music or YouTube Side 2 Elegie [] [] Jay Dee Daugherty The music was written by Allen Lanier, who was a skilled musician, and who actually knew things like, you know, scales and notes. [] Chords. [] Patti Smith It really was my dream to have Chet Baker play at the end, sort of for Jimi. But we couldn’t afford him. It was $5,000, but we didn’t have it. I think our whole budget was $20,000. But I can hear him in my head. I’ve listened to enough Chet Baker to imagine how he would have approached that. [] Michael Stipe I think Patti is really good at embracing joy but also, within that, the sadness of life. And that certainly, at least unconsciously, must have worked its way into my own work. And perhaps I have a similar understanding of the fragility of life, and the beauty of joy, and the heaviness of grief, to be able to tap into what she was singing about in a very direct way. [
